title: Emmaus, slowly (Luke 24:13–35)
hook: stay with us, because it is towards evening

segments.voice: Yesterday, the women at the tomb, and the apostles who heard it as idle tales. Your line was not idle tales. Whose good news did you let be true? Day four hundred eighty-eight.

The same Sunday, in the afternoon. Two disciples are walking away from Jerusalem, toward a village called Emmaus, about sixty furlongs off, seven miles or so. One is named Cleophas. The other Luke never names. They're talking about everything that has happened, the way you talk after a funeral, going over it and over it. A stranger falls into step with them and asks what they're discussing. They stop, faces sad. Are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who doesn't know? Today we walk the road to Emmaus, slowly, because Luke tells it slowly, and the slowness is the point.
screen: `TWO WALKING AWAY.` → `A STRANGER FALLS INTO STEP.` → `ARE YOU THE ONLY ONE WHO DOESN'T KNOW?`

segments.voice: They tell him the whole story, and their saddest line is three words: we had hoped. We hoped it was he that should redeem Israel. Past tense. The stranger answers by walking them through the scriptures, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, showing what they said about the Christ. It takes miles. Then they reach the village, and he makes as if to keep going. And they won't let him. In the Douay-Rheims: "But they constrained him; saying: Stay with us, because it is towards evening, and the day is now far spent. And he went in with them." At table he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them. "And their eyes were opened, and they knew him: and he vanished out of their sight." Afterward they say their hearts were burning while he opened the scriptures on the road, and they run the seven miles back in the dark to tell the others how he was known to them in the breaking of bread. Catholics see the shape of the Mass in this story, and the Church has said so often. First the word: the scriptures opened and explained. Then the table: bread taken, blessed, broken, given. Saint John Paul the Second built his letter for the Year of the Eucharist around this scene and titled it with the disciples' plea in Latin, Mane nobiscum Domine, stay with us, Lord. Notice, too, what doesn't happen. He doesn't force his way in. He would have walked on. The invitation is theirs. Luke shows the risen Christ waiting to be asked.
screen: `WE HAD HOPED.` · `THE SCRIPTURES OPENED ON THE ROAD.` · `STAY WITH US, IT IS TOWARDS EVENING.` · `KNOWN IN THE BREAKING OF BREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: invite Christ to stay tonight. Settle, and breathe. Think back over today as if it were a road. Where were you walking, and what were you talking about? What did you hope for that didn't happen? Let it be there, the way it was for those two. Then picture the evening coming in, the light going. If you pray, you can use their words: stay with us, because it is towards evening. If you don't, just notice what you would want to stay with you tonight. The bell holds the time.
Emmaus. The village seven miles from Jerusalem where two disciples knew the risen Jesus in the breaking of bread. Nobody is certain where it was. Today's word.
Your line: stay with us. Today, at dinner, notice who is at your table, and make one of them welcome to stay a little longer. Day four hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the Emmaus story in Easter week and on the Third Sunday of Easter in one year of the cycle, and the Church often points to it as the pattern of the Mass: the Liturgy of the Word, then the Liturgy of the Eucharist.

fork.setup: you've walked seven miles with a stranger who made the scriptures burn. you reach your village at dusk, and he starts to walk on. what do you do?

ask his name before he goes.
fork.reveal: they constrained him: stay with us, because it is towards evening. he went in, broke the bread, and they knew him.

original.note: Latin, from the Vulgate of Luke 24:29: stay with us. John Paul II's 2004 letter takes its title from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about two people who didn't recognize a friend.
what it means: the risen Christ is known when the scriptures are opened and the bread is broken, and he waits to be invited.
what a scholar hears: the four table verbs (took, blessed, broke, gave) echo the Last Supper; Emmaus's location is still debated.

notes: Sixty furlongs (Douay; stadia) as about seven miles: standard; some manuscripts read 160 stadia. Confirm.
Emmaus's location is uncertain (Emmaus Nicopolis, el-Qubeibeh, Abu Ghosh, Motza and others proposed). Stated as uncertain.
'We had hoped' and the burning hearts (24:21, 24:32) are paraphrased without quotation marks. Confirm.
Lectionary: Emmaus is the Gospel for Wednesday of the Easter Octave and the Third Sunday of Easter, Year A. Confirm the howItsDone phrasing.
Original is Latin (Vulgate), not Greek, because the Catholic devotion and the papal letter use it; confirm this choice.
